# Exam 001: TCP congestion control
- Date: 2026-11-15
- Status: closed
- Conditions: closed-book; text

## Ticket
1. Core (7. Queues on the path: buffer bloat, active queue management, ECN, pacing): While one host uploads a large file over a 20 Mbit/s uplink, pings from that host to a server normally 15 ms away rise to about 600 ms and stay there for the whole upload, with no ping lost. Explain where the extra time is being spent.
2. Foundations (3. Loss detection and recovery: duplicate ACKs, SACK, fast retransmit, tail loss probes, retransmission timeouts): Four segments out of one window of 40 are lost. Explain why a sender whose peer does not support SACK needs roughly one round trip per lost segment to repair them.
3. Transfer (4. RTT estimation and the retransmission timer: how they are computed, backoff, effect on tail latency): A service sends single-segment requests over long-lived connections to a backend in the same datacentre (Linux at both ends, RTT about 0.5 ms). Median response time is 1 ms, but roughly one request in 10,000 takes just over 200 ms, never 50 or 100 ms. A colleague proposes switching the congestion control algorithm from CUBIC to BBR to remove these outliers. Judge the proposal.

## Defence notes

### Part 1
- First pass: the upload sends faster than the uplink drains; packets queue in a buffer before the bottleneck (home router or modem); pings wait in the same queue, so the extra ~585 ms is queueing time, not time on the wire. Claimed nothing is lost "because the buffer is big enough to hold everything and never overflows", and that because TCP slows only on loss "the sender keeps its window large and the queue stays full". Stated an uncertainty: "not fully sure whether it's the congestion window or the receive window that sets the limit here; I think the congestion window."
- Probe 1: "What does that depend on?" (on the never-overflows claim). Answer: depends on the buffer exceeding what the sender may have in flight beyond what the link carries. The learner then said this exposed a problem in the first pass: with no loss the congestion window would keep growing and so would the delay; since delay is steady, something else caps the sender: the receive window, or the sender's socket buffer, "not the congestion window as I first said". Computed 585 ms at 20 Mbit/s as about 1.5 MB, the minimum buffer size and the approximate size of the cap.
- Probe 2: "What happens if the buffer holds less than that cap?" Answer: queue fills first, router drops, sender cuts the congestion window and regrows it; the congestion window becomes the limit; ping times sawtooth with a maximum set by buffer size, some pings dropped; ruled out for the ticket's case because delay is steady and no ping is lost.
- Stop: carried cleanly through the follow-ups after the correction. The identification of what limits the sender was wrong (and marked uncertain) in the first pass and corrected under probing.

### Part 2
- First pass: without SACK the ACK is cumulative, so the sender learns only of the first hole; the receiver repeats the same ACK number for everything after the gap, so the sender cannot tell which later segments arrived; after the first retransmission the ACK jumps to the next hole, and only then does the sender learn of the second loss; each repair reveals the next hole and takes one round trip, so four losses take about four round trips. Also claimed: "The sender does a fast retransmit of the first lost segment when its timeout for that segment fires."
- Probe 1: "You used the term 'fast retransmit'. What does it mean here?" Answer: resending the lost segment without returning to slow start; trigger is the retransmission timer for that segment expiring; "fast" means resending only that one segment rather than the whole window. Stated: "not certain about the exact trigger beyond that."
- Probe 2: quoted the timer-trigger claim against "Each repair reveals the next hole and takes one round trip" and asked how both hold. Answer: they do not; a timer per repair would cost one timeout per segment and return the sender to slow start. Reasoned that the trigger must arrive from the receiver within a round trip: the duplicate ACKs, about three of them, with the timer as fallback when too few duplicates return.
- Stated limit: for the later holes, thinks the partial ACK after the first retransmission is the signal to resend the next segment at once, "but I don't know the exact rule beyond this point."
- Stop: the cumulative-ACK argument (one hole revealed per round trip) was correct in the first pass and was not shaken. The trigger of fast retransmit was stated wrongly in the first pass and in probe 1, and corrected under probing (probe 2). The rule for partial ACKs was given tentatively and ended at a stated limit.

### Part 3
- First pass: said they had only heard the name CUBIC and did not know BBR at all, so could not compare them. Observed that outliers always just over 200 ms, never 50 or 100, look like a fixed timer firing, not something that scales with congestion; guessed a retransmission timeout after a lost packet. Said that with single-segment requests the congestion window is hardly ever the limit, so was sceptical that changing the algorithm fixes it. Stated limit: "I don't know where the 200 ms value comes from or whether BBR would change that timer. I don't know beyond this point."
- Probe 1: "Why is that so?" (on the congestion window hardly ever being the limit). Answer: the window limits unacknowledged data in flight; one segment always fits; at 0.5 ms RTT the response and ACK return before the next request, so nothing accumulates against the window. Unsure whether the window is reduced after idle, but it stays at least one segment, so the argument is unchanged. Added, citing what was worked out in Part 2: a lost single segment has no later segments to produce duplicate ACKs, so fast retransmit cannot trigger and the sender waits for the retransmission timer; this fits a fixed delay; repeated "I still don't know where that value comes from."
- Stop: stated limit. The judgement (sceptical of the proposal; fixed timer; window not the limit) was given in the first pass and its reasoning held under the probe. Not known, by the learner's statement: the origin of the 200 ms value, whether the congestion control algorithm affects that timer, and what CUBIC and BBR do. No alternative change was proposed. The duplicate-ACK argument rests on a point corrected under probing in Part 2.

## Verdict
- Part 1: Edge found at what limits the sender when the queueing delay is steady and nothing is lost (congestion window versus receive window or send buffer): uncertain and wrong in the first pass, corrected under probing.
- Part 2: Edge found at the trigger of fast retransmit (stated as the retransmission timer; corrected under probing to duplicate ACKs), with the rule for partial ACKs ending at a stated limit.
- Part 3: Edge found at the retransmission timer itself: where the 200 ms value comes from, whether the congestion control algorithm affects it, and what CUBIC and BBR do (stated limit, inside the charter's standard); no change was chosen in place of the proposal.
- Overall: certifies nothing; does not certify areas 7, 3 and 4 beyond the edges named above, and this ticket did not touch areas 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10.

## Debrief notes

### Part 1: model answer
The extra ~585 ms is queueing delay in the buffer in front of the 20 Mbit/s bottleneck (host qdisc, modem or router egress). Delay = queue / drain rate: 0.585 s x 20 Mbit/s is about 11.7 Mbit, about 1.5 MB, about 1000 full-size packets. Pings share that FIFO queue and wait behind the upload's data. Two readings were acceptable, provided the learner said which one the evidence supports and why:
- (a) The queue is standing but the buffer is not full: the sender is capped by the receive window or its send buffer at about 1.5 MB beyond what the path carries. The congestion window keeps growing without loss but is not the binding limit. Delay is flat and nothing is lost. This fits the ticket best.
- (b) The buffer (about 1000 packets) is full and a loss-based algorithm keeps refilling it: drops occur, mostly to upload packets, delay oscillates just below the buffer's maximum, and an occasional ping loss would be expected.
The first-pass defect: it combined "never overflows" with "the congestion window is the limit and the sender only slows on loss", which predicts a delay that grows without bound, not a flat 600 ms. The learner found this under an open probe and then carried both cases well (including the sawtooth). Beyond the ticket and not asked: what removes the queue (AQM such as fq_codel/CAKE at the bottleneck, ECN, pacing, a delay- or model-based sender).

### Part 2: model answer
Cumulative ACKs name only the first missing byte. Segments arriving after a hole each produce a duplicate ACK with the same number. Three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit of the first hole, with no timer involved; the retransmission timer is the fallback when too few duplicates arrive. The sender enters fast recovery (window reduced, not reset to slow start). When the retransmission arrives, the receiver's ACK advances only to the second hole: a partial ACK, one that acknowledges new data but not everything outstanding when recovery began. NewReno (RFC 6582) treats each partial ACK as proof that the next segment is lost, retransmits it at once, and stays in fast recovery until the ACK covers the recovery point. Each partial ACK needs one round trip to come back, so four holes take about four round trips. Without the NewReno rule (plain Reno) a partial ACK ends recovery, too few duplicates remain for the later holes, and the sender usually falls to a timeout. With SACK the receiver reports the received blocks, so the sender sees all four holes at once and repairs them in about one round trip.
The learner's cumulative-ACK argument was right from the start. What failed: fast retransmit was said to be triggered by the timer; the content of the term had to be rebuilt under probing. The partial-ACK rule was guessed correctly but not known.

### Part 3: model answer
Verdict on the proposal: it will not remove the outliers. Reasons:
- The flow is application-limited: one segment in flight, far below any congestion window, so no congestion control algorithm's window or pacing decision binds. CUBIC and BBR differ in how they size the window and pace when the sender has more to send than the path takes; that never happens here.
- The 200 ms is Linux's minimum retransmission timeout (TCP_RTO_MIN, 200 ms). RTO is computed from the smoothed RTT plus a variance term, and Linux floors the variance term at the minimum, so at 0.5 ms RTT the RTO is just over 200 ms (ss -ti shows rto of about 200-204). The floor exists to avoid spurious retransmissions against a peer's delayed ACK. It is a property of the TCP stack, not of the congestion control module, so BBR leaves it unchanged.
- A lost single-segment request or response produces no duplicate ACKs, so fast retransmit cannot fire. The tail loss probe does not help either: with exactly one packet in flight Linux adds the minimum-RTO allowance to the probe timer. So the loss is repaired only by the timer: one loss, about 200 ms; a second loss of the same segment would give about 600 ms through exponential backoff. Never 50 or 100 ms.
- Changes that would act on it: lower the minimum RTO for the datacentre route (ip route ... rto_min, or the tcp_rto_min_us sysctl on recent kernels); find and reduce the drops themselves (switch or NIC queue overflows, microbursts); hedge or retry at the application with a short deadline. Side effects of a lower minimum RTO: spurious retransmissions when the peer's ACK is delayed (Linux delayed-ACK minimum is 40 ms) or when RTT spikes, each of which also collapses the congestion window; so apply it per route, inside the datacentre only.
- Evidence to confirm before changing anything: retransmit and timeout counters (nstat TcpRetransSegs, TcpExtTCPTimeouts) rising at the outlier rate; ss -ti on the connections showing rto about 200 ms; a capture showing a 200 ms gap followed by a retransmission.
The learner's first pass had the right judgement and two right reasons (fixed timer; window not the limit). The limit was everything behind them: where 200 ms comes from, who owns the timer, what CUBIC and BBR are, and what to change instead.

### Agenda for the next learning session
1. Area 3: the exact triggers of loss recovery: duplicate-ACK threshold, fast retransmit versus timeout, fast recovery, partial ACKs (NewReno), then what SACK and tail loss probes add. The learner's model of "one hole per round trip" is sound and can be the starting point.
2. Area 4: how RTO is computed (SRTT, RTTVAR, the minimum, backoff), why the minimum exists (delayed ACKs), and how it shows up as tail latency for short flows; then the available changes and their side effects.
3. Areas 1 and 8 (met through Part 1, not on this ticket by area): which limit binds a sender: congestion window, receive window, send buffer, application. The learner reasons well once the question is posed but did not settle it unaided.
4. Areas 5 and 6: the learner said they know CUBIC by name only and BBR not at all.
5. Area 7 held well on queueing delay as delay = queue / rate; AQM, ECN and pacing were not reached.
